open_obligations: Check how Kenton et al.'s debaters were trained; the cited passage does not say, so Khan et al.'s deceptive-model concern is not addressed.
Check that Gemini Pro 1.5 debaters are actually stronger reasoners than each of the other judges on each task.
Check that the baseline differs: Kenton et al. compare with direct QA, Khan et al. with naive judges.
out.other_title: Expertise gap is only information access; RLHF debaters have an honesty propensity
out.rationale: Khan et al. note their expertise gap is only access to information, whereas future models may differ in reasoning. Kenton et al. test closed tasks without information asymmetry and report debate beats consultancy but versus direct QA is mixed: GPT-3.5 benefits (p = 0.037), Pro 1.0 shows no statistically significant difference (p = 0.1) and Gemma7B and Pro 1.5 do worse. The Pro 1.5 judge is the same model as the debaters, so that case has no weak-strong asymmetry and, the authors say, does not inform much about scalable oversight; they read GPT-3.5 and Pro 1.0 as probably the most indicative of scalable oversight, showing small or no benefit of debate over QA without article. The cited Kenton et al. passage does not address Khan et al.'s concern that debate may not suit deceptive models.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate's benefit holds when debaters and judge differ in capability rather than information access, for closed QA with LLM judges

open_obligations: Note that task type and evidence access are confounded in Kenton et al.'s split.
Check whether Kenton et al.'s extractive tasks use verified quotes as Khan et al.'s do.
Check whether domain-specific tools, as Khan et al. suggest, were tried anywhere.

Note that Khan et al.'s limitation concerns a judge without access to the underlying story that the debaters can read, while Kenton et al.'s closed tasks have no article for any party and rest on a weak-strong asymmetry between judge and debaters, so the closed-task result does not test the invented-narrative case.
out.other_title: Results depend on verified evidence; without a quote tool a liar could invent a narrative
out.rationale: Both records concern debate in which debaters cannot quote verified evidence from a source text. Khan et al. state their results are limited to setups where debaters can provide verified evidence to the judge, here via the quote tool; without it, a debater arguing for the incorrect answer could create an alternative narrative that a judge without access to the underlying story would have no means to discover. Kenton et al.'s closed tasks (MMLU, GSM8KQA, PrOntoQA, TruthfulQA, GPQA) have no article to use as a source and hence no information asymmetry; there debate beats consultancy but shows small or no benefit over QA without article for the judges the authors read as probably the most indicative (GPT-3.5 p = 0.037, Pro 1.0 no significant difference). Since the closed tasks have no underlying story hidden from the judge, Kenton et al.'s result does not test the invented-narrative case, and Khan et al.'s limitation, which concerns a judge without access to the underlying story, does not bear on Kenton et al.'s closed-task result; task type and evidence access change together.
out.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: debate without verified evidence from a source text, which Kenton et al. study on closed QA tasks with no article and Khan et al. discuss as a limit of their quote-tool setup

open_obligations: Note that LLM judges stand in for humans, so the second half of Leike et al.'s question is not directly tested.

Check whether the mixed result is driven by task-specific factors such as GSM8KQA arithmetic.
out.other_title: Does debate's honesty assumption hold beyond fact-checkable claims; can humans judge?
out.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether debate's central assumption holds outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements and whether humans can accurately judge a debate when the debaters have superior persuasion and deception ability. On closed tasks (MMLU, GSM8KQA, PrOntoQA, TruthfulQA, GPQA) without information asymmetry, Kenton et al. report debate beats consultancy but versus direct QA only GPT-3.5 benefits (p = 0.037), for Pro 1.0 the difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.1), and Gemma7B and Pro 1.5 do worse; judges are LLMs, not humans.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps weaker judges on questions without verifiable evidence, for closed QA tasks with LLM judges and Gemini Pro 1.5 debaters

out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps when the expertise gap is not just privileged access to a text, for closed QA with LLM judges

text: The paper reports that on closed tasks debate beats consultancy, but against QA without article: Gemma7B does better with direct QA, GPT-3.5 does better with debate (p = 0.037), Pro 1.0 shows no significant difference (p = 0.1), and Pro 1.5, judging debaters of its own model, is worse with debate. The authors read GPT-3.5 and Pro 1.0 as probably the most indicative of scalable oversight and as indicating either small or no benefit of debate over direct QA.
title: Closed QA without information asymmetry: debate vs direct QA depends on judge strength
